What a release means here, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

The releasable unit is the repository, because what ships together sits together — one version, everywhere. The npm package at `packages/lattice`, the marketplace catalogue and both host plugin manifests at the root, the `arch-*` skills under `skills/`, and the VS Code extension at `packages/lattice-vscode` all carry that same version, written by the `extra-files` list below. release-please bumps the root manifest (this repository's own `package.json`), writes the root `CHANGELOG.md`, and tags `v<version>` — the same bare `v*` tags the plugin's releases already carried, which is why the version history continues rather than restarting.

Two things this configuration refuses. The alternative — releasing `packages/lattice` alone — cannot ship the catalogue or the plugin manifests, because release-please rejects `extra-files` paths that climb out of the release unit (`..` is refused: measured on the 0.4.0 release lane, `packages/lattice/../../.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` failed with `illegal pathing characters in path`); making the root the unit is the mechanism that lets one release bump everything. And the extension is not a second component — it was once, and the version chain (docs/skills/versioning.md) is what holds the decision: a client that resolves the server out of the workspace pairs with the engine it is released with, and one version makes the pairing visible instead of a matrix to manage.

`pull-request-title-pattern` overrides the default this repository would reject. release-please titles a release pull request `chore${scope}: release${component} ${version}`, where `${scope}` is the target branch — `chore(main): release 0.5.0`. CI runs commitlint on every pull request title, and `main` is not a valid scope, so the release pull request would fail its own required check and could never merge.
